text.title: Eveline
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A young woman named Eveline sits at her window in Dublin, contemplating her decision to flee her abusive home with her lover Frank, a sailor. As she prepares to board a ship to Buenos Aires, she becomes paralyzed by fear and family obligation, ultimately unable to leave.

eveline.name: Eveline
eveline.description: A young woman over nineteen years old living in Dublin with her abusive father. She works at the Stores and cares for her younger siblings. She has agreed to run away with Frank, a sailor, to Buenos Aires but becomes paralyzed by fear and family obligation at the moment of departure.
eveline.context: Joyce's story is set in early 20th century Dublin, a time of economic hardship and limited opportunities for young women. Eveline represents the paralysis that Joyce saw as characteristic of Dublin life.

frank.name: Frank
frank.description: A kind, manly, open-hearted sailor who has fallen on his feet in Buenos Aires. He courts Eveline, takes her to the theatre, tells her stories of his travels, and plans to marry her and take her to South America. He is present at the final scene, urging her to board the ship.
frank.context: Frank represents the possibility of escape and a different life. His character embodies the romantic ideal of adventure and rescue that appeals to Eveline.

eveline-father.name: Eveline's Father
eveline-father.description: An abusive, aging man who hunts the children from the field with a blackthorn stick, threatens Eveline with violence, squabbles over money on Saturday nights, and forbids her relationship with Frank. He is becoming old and sometimes shows kindness, but his violence and control dominate Eveline's life.
eveline-father.context: Eveline's father represents the patriarchal authority and domestic violence that traps her. His character embodies the obstacles to her escape.

eveline-mother.name: Eveline's Mother
eveline-mother.description: Deceased. She was alive when Eveline was younger and the family went on a picnic to the Hill of Howth. She suffered from an illness and made Eveline promise to keep the home together. She is remembered as having lived a life of commonplace sacrifices ending in craziness. She repeatedly said 'Derevaun Seraun' during her illness.
eveline-mother.context: Eveline's mother is a powerful absent presence in the story. Her memory and the promise Eveline made to her become the ultimate obstacle to Eveline's escape.

data.transitionDescription: Eveline remembers her mother as alive, going on a picnic to the Hill of Howth, and her father putting on her mother's bonnet to make the children laugh.

data.transitionDescription: Eveline recalls her mother's illness, the street organ playing outside, and her mother's voice repeating 'Derevaun Seraun.' She remembers her promise to keep the home together. Her mother's life of commonplace sacrifices and final craziness becomes vivid and binding.

harry.name: Harry
harry.description: Eveline's brother, alive and working in the church decorating business. He is nearly always down somewhere in the country. He sends money when he can but is not present to protect Eveline from their father. She writes a letter to him.
harry.context: Harry represents a brother who has escaped the home but remains emotionally connected through letters and money.

ernest.name: Ernest
ernest.description: Eveline's brother, now deceased. He was too grown up to play with the other children in the field. He was Eveline's favorite brother. He used to go for her like he went for Harry, but he is now dead.
ernest.context: Ernest represents another loss in Eveline's life and the absence of male protection.

miss-gavan.name: Miss Gavan
miss-gavan.description: Eveline's supervisor at the Stores. She treats Eveline poorly, has an edge on her, and is especially cruel when there are people listening. She would be glad if Eveline ran away.
miss-gavan.context: Miss Gavan represents the workplace cruelty and lack of respect that makes Eveline's current life unbearable.

little-keogh.name: Little Keogh
little-keogh.description: A cripple who played with Eveline and the other children in the field. He used to keep nix and call out when he saw Eveline's father coming, warning the children.
little-keogh.context: Little Keogh represents the childhood friendships and games that Eveline has lost.

tizzie-dunn.name: Tizzie Dunn
tizzie-dunn.description: A child who played with Eveline in the field. She is now dead.
tizzie-dunn.context: Tizzie Dunn represents the losses and deaths that have marked Eveline's life.

the-devines.name: The Devines
the-devines.description: A family whose children played with Eveline in the field.
the-devines.context: The Devines represent the community of childhood that has dispersed.

the-waters.name: The Waters
the-waters.description: A family whose children played with Eveline in the field. They have gone back to England.
the-waters.context: The Waters represent the emigration and dispersal of Eveline's childhood community.

the-dunns.name: The Dunns
the-dunns.description: A family whose children played with Eveline in the field.
the-dunns.context: The Dunns represent the community of childhood that has dispersed.

priest-in-photograph.name: Priest in Photograph
priest-in-photograph.description: A school friend of Eveline's father. His yellowing photograph hangs on the wall above the broken harmonium. He is now in Melbourne.
priest-in-photograph.context: The priest represents absent authority and the dispersal of Eveline's father's generation.

man-from-belfast.name: Man from Belfast
man-from-belfast.description: A man who bought the field where Eveline and the other children used to play and built bright brick houses with shining roofs.
man-from-belfast.context: The man from Belfast represents the forces of modernization and development that have destroyed Eveline's childhood world.

man-from-last-house.name: Man from Last House
man-from-last-house.description: A man who passes by on his way home, whose footsteps Eveline hears on the concrete pavement and cinder path.
textMentions: The man out of the last house
man-from-last-house.context: The man from the last house represents the ordinary life of the avenue continuing around Eveline.

young-children.name: Young Children
young-children.description: Two young children left in Eveline's charge. She is responsible for seeing that they go to school regularly and get their meals regularly.
young-children.context: The young children represent Eveline's domestic responsibilities and the reason she must keep the home together.

organ-player.name: Organ Player
organ-player.description: A street organ player who plays outside Eveline's home on the evening she is preparing to leave. The music reminds her of her mother's illness.
organ-player.context: The organ player's music triggers Eveline's memory of her mother's promise and becomes the catalyst for her final paralysis.

north-richmond-st-home.name: Eveline's Home on North Richmond Street
north-richmond-st-home.description: A small brown house on North Richmond Street in Dublin where Eveline lives with her father and younger siblings. The home contains familiar objects she has dusted for years, a broken harmonium, and a yellowing photograph of a priest on the wall.
north-richmond-st-home.context: The home represents both security and imprisonment for Eveline. It is the space she must leave but also the space she cannot abandon.
north-richmond-st-home.climate: Evening, dusty, odour of dusty cretonne
north-richmond-st-home.historicalContext: Early 20th century Dublin, a time of economic hardship and limited opportunities

north-richmond-st-avenue.name: North Richmond Street Avenue
north-richmond-st-avenue.description: The avenue outside Eveline's home, where the evening invades and few people pass. The man from the last house passes on his way home. A street organ plays in the distance.
north-richmond-st-avenue.context: The avenue represents the ordinary world outside Eveline's home, the world she might escape to or remain trapped in.

field.name: The Field
field.description: A field where Eveline and other children used to play every evening with other people's children. It was later bought by a man from Belfast and built upon with bright brick houses with shining roofs, replacing the little brown houses.
field.context: The field represents Eveline's lost childhood and the forces of modernization that have destroyed her world.

the-stores.name: The Stores
the-stores.description: A shop or department store where Eveline works. Miss Gavan is her supervisor. Eveline works hard there and is treated poorly.
the-stores.context: The Stores represent the workplace oppression and lack of respect that makes Eveline's current life unbearable.

main-road-house.name: House on the Main Road
main-road-house.description: A house on the main road where Frank was lodging when Eveline first saw him. She used to visit this house.
textMentions: a house on the main road
main-road-house.context: The main road house is where Eveline's romance with Frank begins.

theatre.name: Theatre
theatre.description: A theatre where Frank takes Eveline to see The Bohemian Girl. She sits in an unaccustomed part of the theatre with him.
theatre.context: The theatre represents a glimpse of a different, more refined life that Frank offers Eveline.

hill-of-howth.name: Hill of Howth
hill-of-howth.description: A location near Dublin where Eveline's family went on a picnic when her mother was alive. Her father put on her mother's bonnet to make the children laugh.
hill-of-howth.context: The Hill of Howth represents a moment of family happiness and maternal presence that Eveline has lost.
hill-of-howth.historicalContext: Past, when Eveline's mother was alive

sickroom.name: Sickroom
sickroom.description: A close dark room at the other side of the hall from Eveline's window, where her mother lay ill. Outside, a street organ played a melancholy air of Italy.
sickroom.context: The sickroom is where Eveline's mother made her promise to keep the home together and where she heard her mother's voice repeating 'Derevaun Seraun.'
sickroom.historicalContext: Past, during her mother's final illness

north-wall-station.name: North Wall Station
north-wall-station.description: A station at the North Wall in Dublin where ships depart. The station is full of soldiers with brown baggages. Through the wide doors of the sheds, a black boat lies beside the quay wall with illumined portholes. A bell clangs. The boat blows a long mournful whistle into the mist.
textMentions: the station at the North Wall
north-wall-station.context: The North Wall Station is the setting for the climactic moment where Eveline must choose to leave or stay. It represents the threshold between her old life and her potential new life.

boat.name: The Boat
boat.description: A night-boat at the North Wall Station that will take Eveline and Frank to Buenos Aires. It is a black mass lying beside the quay wall with illumined portholes. It blows a long mournful whistle into the mist.
boat.context: The boat represents both escape and danger. It is the vehicle that would take Eveline to a new life, but it also represents the unknown and the seas that might drown her.

buenos-ayres.name: Buenos Aires
buenos-ayres.description: A distant unknown country where Frank has a home waiting for Eveline. He has fallen on his feet there and come over to the old country just for a holiday. It is where Eveline would be married and treated with respect.
buenos-ayres.context: Buenos Aires represents the possibility of escape and a new life where Eveline would be treated with respect and married.

straits-of-magellan.name: Straits of Magellan
straits-of-magellan.description: A location that Frank has sailed through. He told Eveline stories of the terrible Patagonians there.
straits-of-magellan.context: The Straits of Magellan represent the exotic and dangerous world that Frank has experienced and that he offers to Eveline.

canada.name: Canada
canada.description: A destination that Frank sailed to as a deck boy on a ship of the Allan Line at a pound a month.
canada.context: Canada represents one of Frank's maritime adventures.

melbourne.context: Melbourne represents the dispersal of Eveline's father's generation and the absence of authority figures.

belfast.name: Belfast

coloured-print.context: The coloured print represents Catholic religious devotion in Eveline's home.

black-leather-purse.name: Black Leather Purse
black-leather-purse.description: A black leather purse that Eveline holds tightly in her hand as she elbows her way through the crowds doing her marketing on Saturday afternoons.
black-leather-purse.context: The black leather purse represents Eveline's responsibility for household finances and her vulnerability in public spaces.
black-leather-purse.culturalSignificance: Symbol of domestic responsibility and vulnerability

peaked-cap.name: Peaked Cap
peaked-cap.description: A peaked cap that Frank wears, pushed back on his head when Eveline first sees him.

peaked-cap.physicalDescription: Peaked cap, pushed back on his head
peaked-cap.culturalSignificance: Symbol of sailor identity and romance

letters.name: Letters

letters.context: The letters represent Eveline's attempt to communicate her departure to her family, though she ultimately cannot leave.
letters.culturalSignificance: Symbol of her decision to leave and her attempt to explain herself

mothers-bonnet.name: Mother's Bonnet
mothers-bonnet.description: A bonnet belonging to Eveline's mother that her father put on to make the children laugh during a picnic at the Hill of Howth.
mothers-bonnet.context: The mother's bonnet represents a moment of paternal kindness and family happiness that Eveline has lost.
mothers-bonnet.culturalSignificance: Symbol of maternal presence and family happiness

toast.context: The toast represents a moment of paternal care that complicates Eveline's view of her father.
toast.culturalSignificance: Symbol of paternal care and complexity

iron-railing.name: Iron Railing
iron-railing.description: An iron railing at the North Wall Station that Eveline grips with both hands in frenzy as Frank urges her to come aboard the boat.
iron-railing.context: The iron railing represents the physical and psychological barrier that prevents Eveline from leaving.
iron-railing.culturalSignificance: Symbol of paralysis and inability to escape

street-organ.name: Street Organ

seven-shillings.culturalSignificance: Symbol of economic dependence and paternal control

childhood-playgroup.context: The childhood playgroup represents the community and happiness that Eveline has lost.

e01-evening-observation.description: Eveline sits at the window watching the evening invade the avenue. Her head is leaned against the window curtains and she inhales the odour of dusty cretonne. She is tired.

e02-man-passing.description: A man from the last house passes on his way home. Eveline hears his footsteps clacking along the concrete pavement and afterwards crunching on the cinder path before the new red houses.

e03-field-memory.description: Eveline recalls that a field used to be where the new red houses now stand. A man from Belfast bought the field and built bright brick houses with shining roofs.

e04-childhood-play.description: Eveline remembers the children of the avenue playing together in the field: the Devines, the Waters, the Dunns, little Keogh the cripple, she and her brothers and sisters. Ernest never played because he was too grown up.

e05-father-hunting.description: Eveline's father used to hunt the children from the field with his blackthorn stick. Little Keogh would keep nix and call out when he saw her father coming.

e06-deaths-and-departures.description: Eveline reflects that everything changes. Her mother is dead. Tizzie Dunn is dead. The Waters have gone back to England. She and her brothers and sisters are all grown up. Now she is going to go away like the others, to leave her home.

e07-home-review.description: Eveline looks round the room, reviewing all its familiar objects which she has dusted once a week for so many years. She wonders where all the dust comes from and whether she will ever see these familiar objects again.

e08-priest-photograph.description: Eveline notices the yellowing photograph of a priest hanging on the wall above the broken harmonium beside the coloured print of the promises made to Blessed Margaret Mary Alacoque. She realizes she has never found out the name of the priest, who was her father's school friend and is now in Melbourne.

e09-departure-decision.description: Eveline has consented to go away and leave her home. She wonders if that is wise and tries to weigh each side of the question.

e10-shelter-and-food.description: Eveline considers that in her home she has shelter and food, and she has those whom she has known all her life about her.

e11-stores-work.description: Eveline reflects that she has to work hard both in the house and at business. She wonders what they would say of her in the Stores when they found out that she had run away with a fellow.

e12-miss-gavan.description: Eveline recalls Miss Gavan's cruel treatment of her at the Stores. Miss Gavan has always had an edge on her, especially when there are people listening. She would not cry many tears at leaving the Stores.

e13-father-violence.description: Eveline reflects that in her new home in Buenos Aires, she would be married and treated with respect, not like her mother. She is over nineteen but sometimes feels herself in danger of her father's violence. She knows it was that that gave her the palpitations. Her father has begun to threaten her and say what he would do to her only for her dead mother's sake.

e14-money-squabbles.description: Eveline reflects that the invariable squabble for money on Saturday nights has begun to weary her unspeakably. She always gives her entire wages—seven shillings—and Harry always sends up what he can, but the trouble is to get any money from her father. He says she used to squander the money, that she had no head, that he wasn't going to give her his hard-earned money to throw about the streets. He is usually fairly bad of a Saturday night. In the end he would give her the money and ask her had she any intention of buying Sunday's dinner.

e15-household-duties.description: Eveline reflects that she had hard work to keep the house together and to see that the two young children who had been left to her charge went to school regularly and got their meals regularly. It was hard work—a hard life—but now that she was about to leave it she did not find it a wholly undesirable life.

e16-frank-meeting.description: Eveline remembers the first time she saw Frank. He was lodging in a house on the main road where she used to visit. He was standing at the gate, his peaked cap pushed back on his head and his hair tumbled forward over a face of bronze. It seemed a few weeks ago.

e17-frank-kindness.description: Eveline recalls that Frank is very kind, manly, and open-hearted. They came to know each other. He used to meet her outside the Stores every evening and see her home.

e18-theatre-visit.description: Eveline recalls that Frank took her to see The Bohemian Girl. She felt elated as she sat in an unaccustomed part of the theatre with him.

e19-sailor-song.description: Eveline recalls that Frank was awfully fond of music and sang a little. People knew that they were courting and, when he sang about the lass that loves a sailor, she always felt pleasantly confused. He used to call her Poppens out of fun.

e20-frank-stories.description: Eveline recalls that Frank had tales of distant countries. He had started as a deck boy at a pound a month on a ship of the Allan Line going out to Canada. He told her the names of the ships he had been on and the names of the different services. He had sailed through the Straits of Magellan and told her stories of the terrible Patagonians. He had fallen on his feet in Buenos Ayres and had come over to the old country just for a holiday.

e21-father-forbids.description: Eveline recalls that her father found out the affair and forbade her to have anything to say to Frank. He said 'I know these sailor chaps.' One day he quarrelled with Frank and after that she had to meet her lover secretly.

e22-letters-in-lap.description: The evening deepens in the avenue. The white of two letters in Eveline's lap grows indistinct. One is to Harry; the other is to her father.

e23-brothers-memory.description: Eveline reflects that Ernest had been her favourite but she liked Harry too. She recalls that her father is becoming old lately and would miss her. Sometimes he could be very nice. Not long before, when she had been laid up for a day, he had read her out a ghost story and made toast for her at the fire.

e24-howth-picnic.description: Eveline recalls another day, when their mother was alive, when they all went for a picnic to the Hill of Howth. She remembered her father putting on her mother's bonnet to make the children laugh.

e25-street-organ.description: Eveline's time is running out but she continues to sit by the window. Down far in the avenue she hears a street organ playing. She knows the air.

e26-mother-promise.description: Eveline realizes that the street organ's air reminds her of the promise to her mother, her promise to keep the home together as long as she could.

e27-mother-illness-memory.description: Eveline remembers the last night of her mother's illness. She was again in the close dark room at the other side of the hall and outside she heard a melancholy air of Italy. The organ-player had been ordered to go away and given sixpence. She remembered her father strutting back into the sickroom saying 'Damned Italians! coming over here!'

e28-mother-voice.description: As Eveline mused, the pitiful vision of her mother's life laid its spell on her—that life of commonplace sacrifices closing in final craziness. She trembled as she heard again her mother's voice saying constantly with foolish insistence 'Derevaun Seraun! Derevaun Seraun!'

e29-station-arrival.description: Eveline stands among the swaying crowd in the station at the North Wall. Frank holds her hand and she knows that he is speaking to her, saying something about the passage over and over again.

e30-frank-speaking.description: Frank speaks to Eveline about the passage over and over again.

e31-soldiers-and-boat.description: The station is full of soldiers with brown baggages. Through the wide doors of the sheds Eveline catches a glimpse of the black mass of the boat, lying in beside the quay wall, with illumined portholes.

e32-eveline-silence.description: Eveline answers nothing. She felt her cheek pale and cold.

e33-prayer.description: Out of a maze of distress, Eveline prayed to God to direct her, to show her what was her duty.

e34-boat-whistle.description: The boat blows a long mournful whistle into the mist.

e35-passage-booked.description: Eveline realizes that if she went, tomorrow she would be on the sea with Frank, steaming towards Buenos Ayres. Their passage had been booked. She wonders if she could still draw back after all he had done for her. Her distress awoke a nausea in her body and she kept moving her lips in silent fervent prayer.

e36-bell-clangs.description: A bell clanged upon Eveline's heart.

e38-seas-image.description: All the seas of the world tumbled about Eveline's heart. Frank was drawing her into them: he would drown her.

e39-iron-railing.description: Eveline gripped with both hands at the iron railing.

e42-eveline-refusal.description: Eveline cries 'No! No! No! It was impossible.' Her hands clutched the iron in frenzy. Amid the seas she sent a cry of anguish!

e43-frank-beyond-barrier.description: Frank rushed beyond the barrier and called to Eveline to follow. He was shouted at to go on but he still called to her.

e44-white-face.description: Eveline set her white face to Frank, passive, like a helpless animal.

e45-no-sign.description: Eveline's eyes gave Frank no sign of love or farewell or recognition.
